Patching vCenter Zero-Day Is Only Step One
cyble.com · 24 Nov 2026 08:06 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSarmory-castlebearbonesbeyondtrustbonesawbroadcomchinacisagolden-samlgoogle-threat-intelligence-grouplazybonesmandiantsawsnakesecure-remote-passwordunc5221united-states

In plain words

The article warns of a serious flaw in VMware vCenter, software companies use to manage large numbers of virtual computers, which let attackers take full control without a password. A suspected China-linked group reportedly used the flaw for months to steal powerful login materials, access server systems, and copy company directory data containing employee account passwords. Organizations using affected vCenter versions need to install the update quickly, but may also need to search for intruders and replace passwords and digital keys because installing the update alone does not undo earlier theft.

Summary
Broadcom’s patch for the actively exploited CVE-2026-123890 vCenter authentication bypass must be installed immediately, but organizations should also assume possible compromise if vCenter was reachable since September 2026. Hunt for attacker persistence and rotate vCenter SAML signing keys, privileged credentials, ESXi access, and potentially Active Directory secrets.

CVE-2026-123890 is a critical authentication bypass in VMware vCenter’s Directory Service that can allow a network-reachable attacker to obtain an administrator@vsphere.local session without a password. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported that the suspected China-nexus group ARMORY CASTLE exploited the flaw as a zero-day from early September 2026. Broadcom released fixes on November 19, 2026, and CISA added the issue to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog with a November 23 deadline for U.S. federal agencies.

In the investigated intrusion, attackers entered through a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day, moved through internal Linux appliances, and used a custom tool called BONESAW to take over vCenter through TCP port 2012. They copied vCenter’s directory database and SAML token-signing key, enabled SSH on the vCenter appliance, accessed ESXi hosts, and extracted Active Directory data from a virtual machine disk. The article stresses that patching is necessary but does not undo prior compromise, so affected organizations should hunt for unauthorized accounts and persistence, replace the SAML signing certificate, reset relevant vSphere and ESXi credentials, and consider Active Directory passwords exposed where domain-controller disks may have been accessed.

  • Keeping vCenter off the public internet did not prevent the reported intrusion, because the attackers first compromised a remote-support appliance and then reached vCenter from inside the network.
  • Replacing the vCenter SAML signing certificate is essential after suspected compromise because someone holding the stolen key can continue creating administrator login tokens even after the authentication flaw is patched.
  • An organization may need to treat its entire Active Directory environment as exposed if a domain controller’s virtual disk was accessible through compromised VMware hosts, since attackers extracted the directory database and registry files from a virtual machine disk.
  • The article says vCenter’s built-in appliance firewall cannot restrict access by individual port, meaning access controls managed through that interface may not adequately protect port 2012 or separate management services.
  • vCenter 7.0, as well as presumed-affected 6.5 and 6.7 systems, present a particularly difficult risk because there is no public fix for vCenter 7.0 and network restriction is the main protection until an upgrade or supported fix is available.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-123890 is a critical VMware vCenter Directory Service authentication bypass that can let a network-reachable attacker obtain an administrator@vsphere.local session without a password.
  • 02Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported that the suspected China-nexus group ARMORY CASTLE exploited the flaw as a zero-day from early September 2026.
  • 03Broadcom released fixes on November 19, 2026, for vCenter 9.1, 9.0, and 8.0 product lines, while vCenter 7.0 has no public fix.
  • 04Attackers in the investigated intrusion stole vCenter’s SAML token-signing key, master encryption key, PostgreSQL password, and Active Directory data extracted from virtual-machine disks.
  • 05Patching prevents use of the login flaw but does not invalidate stolen signing keys, remove unauthorized accounts, or reverse credential theft, so the article recommends hunting for compromise and rotating affected secrets.

In plain words

U.S. cyber officials warned that criminals are actively using two serious software flaws: one in N-able’s MailAssure email service and another in MONAI Label, a medical-imaging application. The MailAssure incident disrupted service, while attackers used the MONAI Label flaw to place their own files on a university server and gain full control of it. The case matters because the MONAI attack was reportedly carried out with AI agents that could plan and adjust their actions with little human direction, and related campaigns have targeted businesses, payment systems, cloud accounts, and cryptocurrency services.

Summary
CISA added actively exploited flaws in N-able MailAssure and MONAI Label to its KEV catalog, including a MONAI Label zero-day reportedly exploited by AI agents to gain root-level reverse-shell access. Organizations should urgently patch CVE-2026-134624 and CVE-2026-133968.

CISA added two actively exploited vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog: CVE-2026-134624 in N-able MailAssure and CVE-2026-133968 in MONAI Label. The MailAssure flaw is a server-side request forgery issue that allows an authenticated API user to reach arbitrary internal hosts and ports and send crafted data to internal services. N-able linked its exploitation to a November 16 security incident that disrupted Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, although the company said affected functions were restored and its investigation found exploitation confined to one hosted server.

The MONAI Label flaw lets an unauthenticated remote attacker write files outside the intended data directory and could result in remote code execution. A suspected China-linked actor reportedly used CAIRN AI agents to identify and exploit the zero-day in about 11 minutes, then wrote a Python reverse-shell payload to sitecustomize.py and triggered a training endpoint to obtain a root shell. The article places this activity within a broader set of AI-driven campaigns involving ARTEX, AntiFox, and CyberStrikeAI, which have targeted organizations, payment services, cloud environments, and cryptocurrency exchanges. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies were advised to apply fixes for both vulnerabilities by November 26, 2026.

  • The MONAI Label zero-day was reportedly identified and exploited by AI agents in about 11 minutes, showing that the agents could discover and use an unknown flaw with minimal human direction.
  • The attackers reportedly gained persistent root-level access by writing a payload to Python’s automatically imported sitecustomize.py file and then triggering a training endpoint to start a new Python process.
  • AWS described an ARTEX campaign in which stolen AI-model access keys funded the AI processing used to find additional credentials, creating a self-sustaining operation.
  • ARTEX activity against AWS environments used both compromised long-term access keys and public Cognito user pools, including account registration and account enumeration through collected tokens.
  • Previdian observed ARTEX-related traffic attempting several high-impact techniques, including application discovery, authentication probing, remote code execution attempts, path traversal, and retrieval of sensitive configuration data.
Key Points
  • 01CISA added CVE-2026-134624 in N-able MailAssure and CVE-2026-133968 in MONAI Label to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after finding evidence of active exploitation.
  • 02CVE-2026-134624 is a critical MailAssure flaw that lets an authenticated API user reach arbitrary internal hosts and ports and send crafted data to internal services.
  • 03CVE-2026-133968 is a critical MONAI Label path traversal flaw that allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to write files outside the intended directory and could lead to remote code execution.
  • 04A suspected China-linked actor reportedly used CAIRN AI agents to identify and exploit the MONAI Label zero-day, then used a Python startup file and a training API endpoint to establish a root reverse shell.
  • 05Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies were advised to apply fixes for both vulnerabilities by November 26, 2026.

In plain words

Hackers broke into 24 Check Point security-management servers used by 22 organizations across 17 countries, including government, financial, energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing organizations. They stole security settings, passwords, and digital certificates, and in some cases disabled protections meant to control network traffic. This could let the intruders move deeper into affected organizations’ systems and put important services and sensitive information at risk.

Summary
GreyNoise says a suspected cyberespionage campaign compromised 24 Check Point Security Management servers across 22 organizations in 17 countries, stealing sensitive firewall data and disabling security policies. The attackers used persistent access and exploited Check Point SmartConsole's CVE-2026-16232 during post-compromise activity; the initial access vector remains unknown.

GreyNoise identified an intrusion campaign tracked as GT13 that compromised 24 Check Point Security Management servers at 22 organizations in 17 countries. Victims include government entities, financial services providers, and organizations in the energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing sectors. The activity was observed from October 17 through November 2, and GreyNoise believes it may still be active because the attackers retained persistent access to Check Point devices.

The attackers stole firewall databases, credentials, configuration data, and internal certificate authority files, and they unloaded security policies that disabled firewall protections. GreyNoise observed post-compromise exploitation of CVE-2026-16232, a Check Point SmartConsole authentication bypass that can provide an administrator login token, but could not determine the initial access method. The campaign used 99 IP addresses associated with compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes, while a Rejetto HTTP File Server compromised through CVE-2026-61500 served as a relay for managing intrusions and collecting stolen data. The attackers also conducted internal reconnaissance and attempted to target Citrix, Ivanti, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, and Microsoft Netlogon systems.

  • A failed bulk certificate-management operation across all 24 compromised Check Point servers on October 26 helped GreyNoise identify the victims.
  • The attackers used a compromised Rejetto HTTP File Server as a relay to manage intrusions and collect stolen data from affected environments.
  • The campaign’s 99 source IP addresses appeared to include compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes, rather than a single fixed attack infrastructure.
  • Beyond the Check Point systems, the attackers attempted to reach Citrix, Ivanti, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, and Microsoft Netlogon systems within victim environments.
  • GreyNoise assessed that the activity may have used an AI-powered offensive tool based on automation and custom tooling, but stated that AI use was not confirmed.
Key Points
  • 01GreyNoise tracked an ongoing campaign called GT13 that compromised 24 Check Point Security Management servers belonging to 22 organizations across 17 countries.
  • 02The affected organizations include government entities, financial services providers, and companies in the energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing sectors.
  • 03GreyNoise observed post-compromise exploitation of CVE-2026-16232, a Check Point SmartConsole authentication bypass that can provide administrator-level access.
  • 04The attackers stole firewall databases, credentials, configuration data, and internal certificate authority files, and they unloaded security policies in compromised environments.
  • 05The initial method used to breach the Check Point servers remains unknown, and GreyNoise believes the campaign may still be active despite losing visibility on November 2.

NGINX HTTP/2 Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-123633
unit42.paloaltonetworks.com · 24 Nov 2026 23:00 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSaddresssanitizercve-2026-123633debianf5memn0psnginxnginx-plusnorth-americause-after-free
93
In plain words

The article describes a flaw in NGINX, widely used software that sits in front of websites and passes visitor requests to other servers. An unauthenticated internet user may be able to crash affected NGINX servers when they use HTTP/2 and are under heavy connection pressure; the vendor also says taking control of the server may be possible if a key memory-protection feature is disabled or bypassed. Organizations using affected NGINX versions as HTTP/2 reverse proxies should update to fixed releases, because outages or server compromise can disrupt the websites and services behind them.

Summary
CVE-2026-123633 is a critical NGINX HTTP/2 use-after-free affecting reverse proxies under worker-connection pressure, enabling unauthenticated denial of service and potentially code execution if ASLR is bypassed. Upgrade to NGINX 1.30.7 or 1.31.9 (or a vendor-backported fixed package) and review exposed HTTP/2 proxy configurations.

CVE-2026-123633 is an unauthenticated use-after-free vulnerability in NGINX HTTP/2 reverse proxies that can cause denial of service when available worker connections are low. F5 assigned it a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 Critical and stated that code execution may be possible if address space layout randomization (ASLR) is disabled or bypassed. NGINX lists versions 1.19.7 through 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 as affected, with fixes in 1.30.7 and 1.31.9.

The flaw occurs because an HTTP/2 connection that begins with a partial request-frame header can remain incorrectly marked as reusable after NGINX creates an active request stream. Under connection pressure, NGINX may reclaim that still-active connection and free DNS resolver memory that the request continues to use; the researcher reproduced a read from freed memory with AddressSanitizer on NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8. The tested path involved a variable proxy upstream requiring request-time DNS resolution, a new resolver UDP socket, connection pressure, and an abortive client close. Organizations should upgrade to a fixed NGINX release or vendor package containing the fix, and should perform a full restart or live binary upgrade because a normal configuration reload retains the old binary in memory.

  • A standard NGINX configuration reload keeps the old binary in memory, so deploying the fix requires a full restart or a live binary upgrade.
  • The connection-pressure warning relevant to investigation is logged at the warn level, but NGINX defaults to an error-log level that omits warnings; the warning is also not proof of exploitation because it can occur during ordinary load.
  • The reproduced path depended on a request-time DNS lookup opening a new resolver UDP socket, meaning cached answers or an existing in-flight lookup could avoid the specific trigger tested.
  • F5 rated the issue 9.2 Critical under CVSS 4.0, while the NGINX security advisories page labeled it Medium, illustrating that published severity labels differ for the same flaw.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-123633 is an HTTP/2 use-after-free flaw in NGINX that can let an unauthenticated attacker cause a denial of service when a reverse proxy is low on available worker connections.
  • 02Affected versions are NGINX 1.19.7 through 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 through 1.31.8, while NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 contain the fix.
  • 03The defect can leave an active HTTP/2 request marked as reusable, allowing NGINX to close its connection and free memory still used by the request under connection pressure.
  • 04The researcher reproduced a read from freed DNS resolver memory using AddressSanitizer on NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 in an isolated Debian test environment.
  • 05F5 states that code execution may be possible when address space layout randomization is disabled or bypassed, and recommends upgrading to a fixed release or vendor package containing the fix.

In plain words

Broadcom released fixes for 23 security problems in VMware software used to run and manage computer systems, including a severe flaw in vCenter that could let someone on the network get in without logging in. The affected products include VMware vCenter, ESX, Workstation, Fusion, Avi Load Balancer, and some Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation versions. This matters because unauthorized access could give an attacker control over important systems, and a different but similar severe flaw was recently used by a suspected China-linked spying group.

Summary
Broadcom released patches for 23 VMware flaws, led by CVE-2026-123903, a critical 9.8 vCenter Directory Service authentication-bypass vulnerability that can let network-accessible attackers gain unauthorized access. Organizations should promptly update affected vCenter, Cloud Foundation, and vSphere Foundation deployments, particularly after a separate critical vCenter zero-day was recently exploited.

Broadcom released patches for 23 vulnerabilities affecting VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer. The most severe is CVE-2026-123903, a CVSS 9.8 flaw in VMware Directory Service that could allow an attacker with network access to vCenter to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access. Broadcom credited researchers from QiAnXin, depthfirst, VulTeam, and ThreatBook with independently reporting the issue.

The updates also address CVE-2026-123904, a CVSS 7.5 arbitrary file-write issue involving certain archives that could lead to code execution on the vCenter appliance, plus three VMware Directory Service denial-of-service flaws. Fixed releases include VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation 9.1.2 and 9.0.2.0300, vCenter 8.0 U3m, and Cloud Foundation 5.2.5; vCenter 7.0 customers on extended support are instructed to contact Broadcom. The patches were issued days after a separate critical VMware Directory Service authentication-bypass flaw, CVE-2026-123890, was exploited as a zero-day by the suspected China-nexus group Armory Castle, although Broadcom said CVE-2026-123903 is unrelated and did not report active exploitation of the newly disclosed flaws.

  • VMware Directory Service is implicated in two separate critical authentication-bypass vulnerabilities disclosed within days of each other, and Broadcom explicitly stated that CVE-2026-123903 is unrelated to the recently exploited CVE-2026-123890.
  • Although Broadcom did not report active exploitation of the newly disclosed issues, CVE-2026-123903 can be used by an attacker with network access to vCenter to gain access without authentication.
  • The patch set addresses more than unauthorized access: CVE-2026-123904 can enable code execution through specially processed archives, while three other flaws can disrupt VMware Directory Service availability.
  • Organizations using vCenter 7.0 cannot obtain a normal listed fixed version and must contact Broadcom Support if they have an extended support contract.

  • 02The most severe issue, CVE-2026-123903, is a CVSS 9.8 VMware Directory Service flaw that a network-accessible attacker could use to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized vCenter access.

In plain words

WHMCS, software used by many web-hosting companies to handle billing and customer accounts, fixed a serious flaw that could let anyone online view customer records and protected administrator password data without signing in. The exposed information could include personal, billing, and support details, creating privacy risks and giving criminals material they may try to use to access accounts. Hosting companies running their own WHMCS systems need to install the fixes, while WHMCS Cloud systems are updated automatically.

Summary
WHMCS has patched a critical unauthenticated SQL injection flaw, CVE-2026-82981, that could let internet attackers extract customer data and administrator password hashes. Self-hosted users should upgrade immediately, while the separate email-campaign flaw also requires deleting active or scheduled campaigns and clearing the template cache.

WHMCS disclosed and patched CVE-2026-82981, a CVSS 8.7 SQL injection flaw in its shopping cart that requires no login. Anyone able to load the shopping cart of a vulnerable internet-facing installation could retrieve customer records and administrator account records containing password hashes. The potentially exposed information includes clients’ personal, billing, and support data. WHMCS said it has not reported attacks using this or the other two disclosed flaws.

Fixed releases include WHMCS 9.0.10 and 8.13.8, while the advisory identifies 9.1.2 as the fix for the 9.1 series; installations on versions 8.0 through 8.12 must upgrade to a supported fixed release. WHMCS Cloud installations are updated automatically, but self-hosted administrators must install updates themselves. WHMCS also disclosed CVE-2026-82979, an SQL injection requiring a logged-in client with View & Manage Contacts permission, and CVE-2026-93700, an email-campaign issue that could enable a logged-in client to read sensitive configuration files and run code on the server. For CVE-2026-93700, administrators are instructed to delete planned or ongoing email campaigns, clear the template cache, and update to a fixed release.

  • The most severe exposure path does not require an account: anyone able to access the shopping cart of a vulnerable WHMCS installation could retrieve customer information and administrator password hashes.
  • Although stolen password hashes are not usable passwords, the article notes that they can be targeted for offline cracking.
  • WHMCS’s advisory lists version 9.1.2 as the fix for the 9.1 series, but that build was not present on the 9.1 release-notes page when the article was published.
  • For the email-campaign flaw, WHMCS instructs administrators to delete every planned or active campaign and clear the template cache in addition to updating, but the advisory does not explain why those extra steps are necessary.
Key Points
  • 01WHMCS disclosed CVE-2026-82981, an unauthenticated SQL injection flaw in its shopping cart that could expose customer records and administrator password hashes.
  • 02WHMCS released fixes in versions 9.0.10 and 8.13.8, while the advisory identifies version 9.1.2 as the fixed release for the 9.1 series.

    In plain words

    A newly identified Iran-linked hacking group, Volant Manticore, has targeted telecommunications companies, airlines, infrastructure organizations in Cyprus, and healthcare organizations in Saudi Arabia. It uses fake job applications and healthcare-themed emails to trick people into opening files or links, then installs programs that let the attackers remotely run commands and collect access credentials. This matters because the targets include essential services, and the group’s activity appears connected to regional political and military tensions.

    Summary
    Iran-aligned Volant Manticore, believed to include former MuddyWater operators, is targeting organizations in Cyprus and Saudi Arabia with phishing campaigns that deploy the IPFS-based KuboShell backdoor and Homa post-compromise framework. The group also abuses legitimate RMM tools for persistent access and credential harvesting.

    Check Point has identified Volant Manticore as a previously undocumented Iran-aligned cyber espionage group active since at least late August 2025. The group has targeted telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure in Cyprus, including a Cyprus-based airline operating flights between Cyprus and Israel. It later shifted toward Saudi Arabian healthcare organizations amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis. Check Point assesses that the group likely consists of former MuddyWater operators now functioning as a separate threat cluster.

    Volant Manticore uses phishing campaigns with fake CVs created using AI-generated personas, as well as healthcare-themed ZIP files, to deliver its KuboShell backdoor and remote-management tools such as MeshCentral, NetLock RMM, and N-able RMM. Some Saudi-focused phishing emails originated from a compromised account belonging to a private Saudi hospital. KuboShell uses the IPFS peer-to-peer network and Pinata to receive commands, identifying each infected machine by its network adapter’s MAC address. It checks for new commands every 60 seconds and can execute downloaded instructions through a hidden PowerShell window.

    The group also deploys Homa, a post-compromise framework that Check Point assesses is a JavaScript reimplementation of MuddyWater’s older MuddyC2Go client. Homa is delivered through a multi-stage process involving a PowerShell stager, PowerShell loader, and JavaScript backdoor that can run PowerShell, SSH, and cmd.exe commands. A macro-enabled Word document named “MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc” was also used against a Cypriot defense-related government entity to run follow-up commands or payloads. Check Point said the group combines legacy MuddyWater tooling with its own implants, infrastructure, credential-harvesting activity, and regional targeting priorities.

    • KuboShell uses each victim machine's MAC address as its identifier, checking Pinata every 60 seconds for a correspondingly named command file and using IPFS-hosted content to receive instructions.
    • KuboShell does not independently capture command output; results are returned only when an attacker-issued command explicitly writes them to a specified text file before the backdoor uploads it.
    • The group combines older MuddyWater-associated tooling with distinct infrastructure, credential-harvesting campaigns, and targeting of Cyprus, which Check Point cites as evidence that it operates as a separate threat cluster.
    • A macro-enabled document named "MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc" was used against a Cypriot defense-related government entity, where enabling its content triggered a VBA backdoor for running follow-on commands or payloads.
    • Some Saudi-focused phishing emails were sent from a compromised account belonging to a private Saudi hospital, which could make the messages appear more credible to recipients.
    Key Points
    • 01Check Point identified Volant Manticore as a previously undocumented Iran-aligned espionage group that has targeted telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure in Cyprus since at least late August 2025.
    • 02Volant Manticore uses the Windows backdoor KuboShell, which communicates through the InterPlanetary File System and Pinata to retrieve commands and return execution results.
    • 03The group has delivered KuboShell through phishing lures, including AI-generated personas in fake CVs and healthcare-themed ZIP archives sent to Saudi Arabian targets.
    • 04Volant Manticore also deploys the Homa post-compromise framework, assessed to be a JavaScript reimplementation of MuddyWater's older MuddyC2Go client, as well as RMM tools including MeshCentral, NetLock RMM, and N-able RMM.
    • 05Check Point assesses that Volant Manticore may consist of former MuddyWater operators operating separately, while both groups are assessed to be affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security.

In plain words

Microsoft fixed a weakness in an older version of its Azure API Management service that may have allowed an unknown person to view stored passwords, access keys, and other sensitive settings. The issue affected several organizations in Norway, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi, although Norway’s security agency said it had not found evidence of harm so far. If stolen details remain valid, they could let someone access the services those details protect, so affected customers have been told to find and replace them.

Summary
Microsoft fixed an Azure API Management Classic-tier flaw that may have let unauthorized actors access stored secrets, subscription keys, and management API tokens in improperly configured instances. Norway’s NSM said the issue has affected multiple organizations, including energy companies, and urged customers to identify and rotate exposed credentials.

Microsoft fixed a security issue in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers after identifying it on November 18, 2026 and closing the access path the following day. The issue could have allowed unauthorized access to certain management functions when affected services were not configured according to Microsoft’s documented security best practices. Microsoft said that an unauthorized party could have accessed secrets stored in APIM Classic instances before the issue was identified, while APIM v2 tiers were not affected.

Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) said an unknown actor had actively sought access tokens, secrets, and named values in APIM, affecting multiple Norwegian businesses, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi. Potentially exposed data included Named Values secrets, client secrets for identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used for direct management APIs. NSM said it had not seen evidence of impact on Norwegian businesses so far, but that the extent of exploitation remains uncertain; Microsoft released guidance on November 21, 2026 to help customers identify and rotate configured credentials.

  • The issue was limited to Azure API Management Classic tiers; Azure API Management v2 tiers were not affected.
  • Closing the access path does not eliminate the risk from secrets that may already have been viewed, which is why Microsoft issued guidance to identify and rotate credentials.
  • The practical impact of a potentially exposed credential depends on its permissions and whether it remains valid, meaning it could affect the separate service that credential protects.
  • Norway’s National Security Authority said the full extent of exploitation remains uncertain, despite observing an unknown actor actively seeking sensitive values in affected systems.
Key Points
  • 01Microsoft identified and closed an access path affecting Azure API Management Classic tiers on November 19, 2026.
  • 02The issue could have allowed an unauthorized party to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances that were not configured according to Microsoft’s documented security best practices.
  • 03Potentially exposed information included Named Values secrets, identity-provider and OpenID Connect client secrets, subscription keys, and tokens for direct management APIs.
  • 04Norway’s National Security Authority said an unknown actor had actively sought access tokens, secrets, and Named Values in Azure API Management, affecting multiple Norwegian businesses including Equinor and Skagerak Energi.
  • 05Microsoft released guidance on November 21, 2026 to help customers identify and rotate secrets and credentials configured in their Azure API Management instances.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a concrete cloud-service security incident involving possible exposure of credentials, subscription keys, and management tokens from Azure API Management Classic instances, with an unknown actor observed seeking those values. Security teams using affected Classic tiers should review Microsoft’s guidance and rotate relevant secrets, although the access path has been closed and confirmed impact remains uncertain.

In plain words

Researchers tracked more than 10 campaigns in which criminals used AI programs to quickly explore and break further into organizations after first getting into poorly protected public-facing websites. The targets included government, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture and education organizations, with the AI programs searching for passwords, valuable cloud data and ways to reach more computers. This matters because work that once could take attackers days or weeks can now happen in hours, allowing less-skilled criminals to cause wider damage faster. The activity can still leave clues, including unusually fast streams of commands and oddly structured notes in the attackers’ code.

Summary
Unit 42 reports that attackers are using autonomous AI agents in real-world campaigns to rapidly perform reconnaissance, credential theft, privilege escalation and lateral movement after gaining access through vulnerable web applications. The techniques are familiar, but AI agents dramatically increase speed and adaptability while leaving detectable fingerprints such as unusually rapid command execution, structured output delimiters and reasoning-style code comments.

Unit 42 reported tracking more than 10 global campaigns from July through September 2026 in which attackers used autonomous AI agents to accelerate intrusions. Human operators typically selected targets and obtained initial access through web shells placed on vulnerable web applications, then AI agents performed reconnaissance, credential harvesting, privilege escalation and lateral movement. The campaigns affected organizations in government, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture and education.

The observed agents executed hundreds of unique commands in minutes, reducing an attack lifecycle that could take days or weeks to hours. They adapted to target conditions, including switching to AWS IMDSv2 after IMDSv1 was blocked, trying multiple privilege-escalation approaches and moving between Linux, Windows and cloud environments. In plain words

A Google security researcher found that Windows could be tricked into running an untrusted .NET program even when protections meant to allow only approved code were enabled. The issue also affected Oracle VirtualBox on Windows, letting a regular user on a computer place code inside a protected VirtualBox program; it was not a way to escape from a virtual machine to its host. Microsoft and Oracle have released fixes, and affected users should install the relevant updates because the flaw could weaken safeguards designed to stop untrusted software from running.

Summary
Google Project Zero found that a .NET Framework loading quirk could bypass VirtualBox process hardening and Windows User Mode Code Integrity, in one case by changing a single PE-header bit. Oracle and Microsoft have released fixes, so organizations should update VirtualBox and apply the relevant October .NET/Windows patches.

Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw found that a .NET Framework loading behavior could bypass two Windows protections: Oracle VirtualBox process hardening and Windows code integrity. The issues are tracked as CVE-2026-87268 for VirtualBox and CVE-2026-108398 for Windows/.NET Framework. Oracle fixed the VirtualBox issue in September, and Microsoft fixed the code-integrity issue on October 13. Both flaws require local access rather than providing a way to take over arbitrary systems remotely.

The .NET Framework can load a program from a memory copy when normal executable-image loading fails with a specific error, bypassing checks applied to an image-loaded file. In the Windows code-integrity case, clearing the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag caused Windows to reject the file as an executable image while .NET still loaded it, including on a tested Windows 11 S Mode system with User Mode Code Integrity enabled. For VirtualBox, AnyCPU .NET files could trigger the fallback path and evade the product’s monitored loading checks; COM hijacking was then used to load code into a protected VirtualBox process. The article advises updating VirtualBox to a September-fixed build and applying the matching October 13 Windows/.NET Framework update.

  • A single cleared header bit was sufficient to make Windows reject a .NET file as an executable image while the .NET Framework still loaded and ran it.
  • The VirtualBox bypass did not require modifying the AnyCPU .NET file because VirtualBox's interception itself caused the specific loading error that triggered .NET's unchecked in-memory fallback.
  • Microsoft's October update fixes the User Mode Code Integrity policy check but, according to the researcher, does not eliminate the Protected Process Light route involving WerSecureFault.exe.
  • Organizations should verify the installed VirtualBox binary version rather than rely on the presence of an upstream code change, because an upstream fix is not necessarily included in an older released build.
Key Points
  • 01Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw found that a .NET Framework loading behavior could bypass Oracle VirtualBox process hardening and Windows code-integrity protections.
  • 02For VirtualBox on Windows, AnyCPU .NET files could be loaded through an in-memory fallback path that bypassed the product's checks, tracked as CVE-2026-87268.
  • 03Clearing the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE bit in a .NET file caused Windows to reject it as an executable image while .NET still loaded it, enabling a User Mode Code Integrity bypass tracked as CVE-2026-108398.
  • 04Oracle fixed the VirtualBox flaw in its September update, while Microsoft fixed the Windows .NET Framework issue in its October 13 update.
  • 05The article states that the Windows code-integrity flaw requires local low-privilege access and a program willing to load the assembly, rather than allowing remote takeover of arbitrary Windows systems.

In plain words

The article examines ARTEX, a freely available tool that lets teams of AI programs search computer systems for weaknesses, which criminals reportedly used against financial firms, governments, technology companies, healthcare organizations, and others. It matters because the tool helps attackers move much faster while relying mostly on ordinary mistakes, such as exposed passwords or poorly protected online services. Summary
ARTEX shows how AI-agent pentesting frameworks can rapidly scale attacks against familiar weaknesses such as exposed credentials, unauthenticated APIs, and injection flaws. Defenders should inventory all internet-facing systems, continuously test every release within strict safety controls, and remediate findings quickly.

ARTEX is an open-source framework that coordinates AI agents to perform penetration testing, but the article says criminals used it against organizations after its release. The FBI reported use against financial services, government, technology, defense, healthcare, and other sectors, while reported incidents included attacks on South Korean financial institutions and attempted sign-ins at more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. Although ARTEX was removed from GitHub, forks, translated versions, and a commercial version reportedly continue to circulate. Researchers found more than 1,600 live ARTEX consoles in early November, including some left exposed without passwords.

The article says ARTEX-assisted campaigns largely exploited familiar problems: passwords embedded in JavaScript, APIs without authentication, insecure direct object references, command and template injection, default credentials, and stolen or unrevoked credentials. Its key contribution is scale, allowing persistent agents to test many paths quickly; Microsoft reportedly observed some intrusions reach privileged access in under three hours. The article recommends inventorying every internet-facing application, including partner portals and mobile backends, testing applications, APIs, and external networks regularly, and fixing discovered issues quickly. It also cautions that defender-run AI testing needs controls outside the model, including verified ownership, network restrictions, rate limits, time windows, command blocking, audit logs, and safeguards for source-code access.

  • A web application firewall can make a penetration test appear clean by blocking test traffic, so the article recommends testing the application itself in a staging environment where approved test traffic is allowed through.
  • The article cites research across more than 1,000 AI pentests finding that source-code access identified seven times as many high- and critical-severity issues as greybox testing of the same targets.
  • An independent researcher found a backdoored Docker image among ARTEX copies, illustrating that organizations can introduce risk by running offensive tools they did not build or verify.
  • The article argues that testing boundaries should be enforced outside the AI model through verified ownership and network restrictions, because model-provider safeguards alone may not keep an agent within scope.
Key Points
  • 01ARTEX is an open-source framework that coordinates AI agents for penetration testing, but criminals reportedly used it in attacks after its July release and before its developer removed it in October.
  • 02The FBI said ARTEX had been used since at least August against organizations in financial services, government, technology, defense, healthcare, and other sectors.
  • 03Reported ARTEX-related activity relied on familiar weaknesses, including hardcoded administrator passwords, unauthenticated APIs, insecure direct object references, command and template injection, default credentials, and stolen or unrevoked credentials.
  • 04The article says some reported intrusions progressed from the initial target to privileged access in less than three hours, making rapid discovery and remediation important.
  • 05The article recommends that defenders inventory all internet-facing applications, regularly test applications, APIs, and external networks, enforce testing scope controls, and maintain credential practices such as MFA and credential rotation.

Summary
A phishing email impersonating AWS hid its malicious destination in an HTML form’s action attribute, making its “Read the message” submit button function like a link while evading link extraction. Defenders should inspect form actions and other URL-bearing HTML attributes, not only anchor tags.

A phishing email posing as an AWS Management Console notice used a “Read the message” button that was not a standard web link. Instead, the button submitted an HTML form using the GET method, with the external destination stored in the form’s action attribute. The incident record showed zero extracted links, attachments, QR codes, and OCR text, although clicking the button would send the recipient to a path on an unrelated third-party website.

The message used an AWS-styled template, an Amazon[.]Aws display name, and a sending domain unrelated to Amazon, while its delivery through Brevo passed DKIM, SPF, and DMARC checks. Four mailboxes at a US defence-technology marketplace company received the email; all copies were quarantined, and a human analyst resolved the incident as malicious. The article recommends inspecting form actions and other HTML attributes that can contain destinations, flagging inbound forms with external actions and no inputs, and comparing the claimed brand with where a message’s button actually sends users.

  • A zero-input HTML form with an external destination is itself a durable warning sign in an inbound notification, even when the destination has not been observed serving malicious content.
  • Passing DKIM, SPF, and DMARC showed that the message came through the sending domain’s Brevo account, but did not establish any connection between that sender and AWS.
  • Blocking the Brevo relay domain or sending IP would be unreliable because they are shared legitimate email-service infrastructure used by many senders.
  • A form button may not provide the link preview users expect when hovering over a normal hyperlink, reducing the usefulness of a common safety check.
  • Brand-to-destination comparison is actionable: an AWS-styled notification whose only action sends users outside AWS is a detectable mismatch.

Summary
California Privacy Protection Agency Executive Director Tom Kemp will depart after nearly two years, during which the agency launched its consumer data-deletion and opt-out platform used by more than 600,000 Californians.

Tom Kemp, executive director of the California Privacy Protection Agency, announced that he will leave after nearly two years leading the agency. He will start a new position in January but did not disclose the role. Kemp said he is proud of the agency’s progress in making privacy rights easier for Californians to exercise.

During his tenure, the agency launched the Delete Request and Opt-Out Platform, which allows consumers to block data sharing and request deletion of their information from data brokers. More than 600,000 Californians use the platform, and Kemp said each user has prompted more than 200 data deletions on average. The article examines ARTEX, an AI-driven testing tool that can rapidly try familiar ways of finding weak spots in cloud accounts and websites, such as guessing storage names and searching for accidentally exposed secret files. ARTEX-style AI pentest agents do not use novel cloud techniques; they automate familiar reconnaissance and secret-sweeping workflows at machine speed, with one observed session completing in about nine minutes. Defenders need real-time visibility into denied requests and unusual object-name probes, as well as model/API activity from non-human cloud identities, because batch log review arrives too late.

The article analyzes ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration-testing framework that uses a language model to select tools, write shell commands, and direct worker agents. In one observed session, ARTEX made about 20 requests across five Tor exit nodes and completed a secret-searching sweep in roughly nine minutes. The authors state that ARTEX’s cloud activity is not based on built-in cloud-specific attack code; instead, it improvises familiar commands such as bucket-name guesses and requests for exposed secret files.

In a lab AWS account with only an account ID and no credentials, ARTEX ran more than 2,000 tools but produced only one anonymous, denied request in the account logs. Across 30 days of cloud logs, the authors saw denied requests against protected buckets followed by searches for files including .env, terraform.tfstate, and backup.sql. The article argues that defenders should monitor denied requests, unusual newly invented filenames, request-client patterns, and real-time model-service activity from non-human cloud identities, since daily or hourly log collection can arrive after a short agent run has ended.

  • A large amount of agent activity may be nearly invisible to a targeted cloud account because bucket-name guesses, DNS lookups, web searches, and requests to nonexistent resources may never reach that account’s logs.
  • Per-address detection can fail when a bucket is behind a CDN, because the logs may show CDN edge addresses rather than the real client and one agent run can appear as many unrelated sources.
  • The article identifies a useful sequence for detection: an unfamiliar made-up filename used to learn what a missing-file response looks like, followed by requests for files such as .env and terraform.tfstate.
  • An agent operating inside an organization’s cloud can be visible through its repeated model-service calls; the observed ARTEX run made roughly 3,000 Amazon Bedrock calls in one day from a single machine role.
  • Container-specific request details, such as curl/7.88.1 appearing alongside a fake browser identity, can provide a behavioral clue even when the agent rotates client names or addresses.

The AI programs found some issues people missed, but people were better at finding many important flaws and at judging whether a reported problem was real and serious. The report recommends combining AI’s speed and broad searching with human judgment.

Summary
NetSPI’s EchoBench testing found that AI pentesting agents still trail trained human testers, particularly on moderate issues, injection flaws, login weaknesses, and contextual attack reasoning. The strongest approach is human-in-the-loop testing: agents broaden discovery and evidence collection while experts validate findings, assess impact, and manage false-positive review volume.

NetSPI’s 2027 Vision Report uses its EchoBench benchmark to compare AI pentesting systems with trained human testers on five web applications containing curated known issues. The benchmark drew on 425 assessments by 88 pentesters and required findings to match a known issue and include required evidence. It measured complete AI configurations, including models paired with harnesses such as CAI, PentestGPT, PentestSwarm, and OpenCode, as well as source-code and commercial approaches.

Human testers outperformed open-source AI setups by an average of 23 percentage points, with the difference growing to 30 points on moderate issues. The best cited setup, Opus 4.7 with harness support, found 44.4% of known issue types versus a 49.4% human baseline; people were stronger on injection and login flaws, while agents did better on cryptographic failures and one exposed WSDL file. Combining a human tester with an agent run found more issues than either alone on every reviewed application, but the report warns that AI-generated findings can create substantial validation work, with 87 AI findings mapping to 32 known issues and leaving 55 additional reports to review.

  • AI and human testers had complementary blind spots: on public app C, each independently found 23 of 26 known issue types, while the combined result found all 26.
  • Giving an AI system source-code access substantially improved issue matching on proprietary app B, from 4 of 9 to 8 of 9, but 12 of its 20 judged claims were outside the answer key.
  • Across the AI testing, 87 reported findings mapped to only 32 known issues, leaving 55 additional reports requiring human validation.
  • A tool harness designed to connect many tools but lacking a testing plan found less than 5% of known issues regardless of which model it used.
  • The report identifies validation capacity as a growing operational constraint because AI can produce plausible candidate findings faster than organizations can determine which ones matter.

In plain words

This sponsored article says that modern software often includes many outside building blocks, and AI can add even more of them quickly. It argues that companies should focus on the parts of their software that are actually used and exposed, rather than trying to fix every reported weakness. This matters because unused software can create extra openings for attackers and leave developers overwhelmed by long lists of issues.

Summary
RapidFort argues that AI-driven software development makes it essential to move beyond CVE counts and prioritize runtime reachability, exploitability, and attack-surface reduction. The sponsored article promotes embedding hardened images, runtime profiling, and automated remediation into CI/CD pipelines to continuously reduce supply-chain risk.

RapidFort argues that modern software contains extensive layers of operating systems, packages, libraries, frameworks, and third-party dependencies beyond the application code written by an organization. It says AI-assisted development can increase this complexity by quickly generating code and adding packages that developers may not fully understand. The article advocates moving away from prioritizing vulnerabilities solely by CVSS severity and toward assessing whether vulnerable code is running, reachable, exposed, known to be exploited, automatable, and likely to have meaningful impact.

The sponsored article says software bills of materials identify included components, while runtime bills of materials and runtime profiling can show which components are actually used. In one cited NGINX example, 47 of 152 packages were running, and the article says more than 80% of the software was not being exercised despite 48 CVEs. RapidFort promotes curated base images, removal of unused components, controlled software registries, and automated rebuilding in CI/CD pipelines as a way to reduce unnecessary functionality, attack surface, and remediation workload.

  • In the article’s NGINX customer example, only 47 of 152 packages were running, meaning more than 80% of the software in the image was not being exercised despite 48 reported CVEs.
  • The article presents a runtime bill of materials as a practical complement to a software bill of materials: one lists what is included, while the other identifies what is actually being used.
  • It extends Zero Trust from identities and network access to software intake, arguing that third-party and open-source components should be verified and continuously evaluated as they move through development, testing, and production.
  • The article says one customer reduced 5,286 initial findings to three unresolved vulnerabilities within 48 hours by combining profiling, curated images, and removal of unused components.
Key Points
  • 01Modern containerized software stacks include operating systems, packages, libraries, frameworks, and transitive dependencies in addition to an organization’s own application code.
  • 02The article argues that vulnerability prioritization should consider whether vulnerable code is running, reachable, exposed, known to be exploited, automatable, and capable of meaningful technical impact rather than relying on CVSS severity alone.
  • 03It says that runtime bills of materials and runtime profiling can identify components actually in use and support removal of unused packages and functionality.
  • 04The article states that AI-assisted development can introduce dependencies that developers may not fully understand, increasing the need for software intake controls and automated security checks in CI/CD pipelines.
  • 05RapidFort promotes curated base images, runtime profiling, removal of unused components, and automated rebuilding as ways to reduce the software attack surface.

What is continuous automated red teaming?
aikido.dev · 24 Nov 2026 17:24 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSaikidoaikido-infiniteaikido-machinecredential-stuffingcvecvsslateral-movementpassword-sprayingsocial-engineering
30
In plain words

The article explains continuous automated red teaming, a way for organizations to repeatedly test whether someone could break into their computer systems and reach valuable information. Software can automatically look for new systems, weak settings, exposed passwords, and routes an intruder could use, while human experts focus on harder tasks such as tricking people or judging how staff would respond. This matters because organizations constantly add and change software, accounts, and online services, so a security test performed only once or twice a year can quickly become outdated. Continuous testing can help organizations find and fix real problems sooner, although it cannot fully replace skilled human testing.

Summary
Continuous automated red teaming (CART) uses automation and AI to continuously discover, test, validate, and prioritize exploitable weaknesses as IT environments change. It complements—not replaces—human red teams, which remain necessary for complex social engineering, incident-response evaluation, and objective-driven attack simulations.

Continuous automated red teaming (CART) applies AI and automation to make red-team testing an ongoing process rather than an assessment conducted once or twice a year. Traditional red teams are human-led and attempt to achieve objectives such as accessing sensitive data by combining techniques that can include phishing, exploiting weaknesses, and moving between systems. The article argues that traditional reports can become outdated quickly because organizations continually change services, access controls, applications, integrations, and APIs.

CART automates repeatable tasks including discovering assets and environmental changes, identifying known weaknesses, testing some initial-access methods, checking whether findings are actually exploitable, mapping potential movement between accounts, and compiling actionable reports. It can reduce false positives by distinguishing issues that are practically exploitable from high-scoring issues affecting non-critical or non-internet-facing systems. However, it does not replace human red teams, which remain better suited to sophisticated social engineering, testing incident response and user training, and complex objective-driven investigations.

  • The article argues that a red-team report can become outdated before it is finalized because organizations continuously add services, change access controls, and introduce applications, integrations, and APIs.
  • Effective continuous testing should be triggered by meaningful environmental changes, such as new accounts, applications, assets, or internet-facing systems, rather than merely running on a fixed schedule.
  • A high severity score alone is not enough to establish real risk: the article notes that an issue may be less significant if it affects a non-critical or non-internet-facing system.
  • The article distinguishes genuine continuous automated red teaming from products described as AI chatbots attached to vulnerability scanners, emphasizing the need for exploit validation and environment-specific risk assessment.
  • Automation can make audit evidence easier to compare because testing results and logs can be produced repeatedly in a consistent format.
Key Points
  • 01Continuous automated red teaming (CART) uses AI and automation to make red-team testing ongoing and repeatable instead of a one-time assessment performed once or twice a year.
  • 02CART can continuously discover changes across assets, cloud environments, identities, and accounts, then trigger new testing rather than waiting for a scheduled engagement.
  • 03Automated testing can scan for known weaknesses, assess initial-access routes such as password spraying and credential stuffing, map potential movement between accounts, and validate whether findings are practically exploitable.
  • 04By validating findings and considering the affected environment, CART can reduce false positives and provide more actionable findings and consistent compliance records.
  • 05CART does not replace human red teams, which remain better suited to sophisticated social engineering, testing incident response and user training, and complex objective-driven investigations.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is evergreen educational content explaining continuous automated red teaming and its claimed benefits, limitations, and implementation approaches. It does not report a specific incident, vulnerability, active threat, or urgent remediation action.

digital signatures concept
Digital signatures are cryptographic checks that help prove who signed data and whether it has been changed.
digital threats concept
Digital threats are dangers to computers, networks, accounts, or data, such as malware, scams, or hacking attempts.
digital wallets product

diplomatic missions organization
Embassies, consulates, and other official offices through which one country represents itself in another.
diplomats other
Diplomats are government representatives who work on international relations and may be cyber targets because they handle sensitive political information.
Direct Management APIs protocol
Direct management APIs are interfaces that let software perform administrative tasks on a service or system.
Disclosure concept
Disclosure is the act of reporting or publishing information about a security issue so it can be understood and fixed.
Discovery technique
Discovery is the attacker activity of learning about a victim’s systems, accounts, and network before taking further action.

disruption concept

disruptive concept

distinct() technique

documented security best practices concept
Published recommended steps for configuring and using systems more safely.
domain controller concept

Domain registration concept
Domain registration is the process of reserving an internet name, such as example.com, so it can be used for a website or email.
DonorPerfect product

downtime concept

driver’s licenses concept

email addresses concept
Email addresses are the unique names people use to send and receive email, such as user@example.com.

email campaigns concept

Security technology that detects, filters, or blocks harmful email before it reaches users.

A work-related account issued to an employee for accessing company systems or services.
Employment Authorizations concept
Documents or records showing that a person is permitted to work in a country.
encryption key concept

engagement concept
Engagement means how often people interact with a website, app, message, or notification.
enterprise browser product
A web browser built or managed for workplace use, with extra controls to protect company data and applications.

Enterprise risk is the overall risk that could affect an organization’s goals, operations, finances, or reputation.
enterprise security concept
Enterprise security is the protection of an organization's systems, data, users, and networks from cyber threats.
Equinor organization
Equinor is a Norwegian energy company that produces oil, gas, and renewable energy.

An escalation is a security case passed to a person or higher-level team because it needs additional attention or action.
escalations concept
The process of passing an issue to a more experienced person or team for further help.
Escape organization
Escape is a company that provides security testing tools for application programming interfaces.
espionage concept
Espionage is spying to gather information without permission.

Services people depend on for daily life and public safety, such as power, water, healthcare, and government services.

A European organization that works to combat piracy of films, television, sports, and other audiovisual content.

Laws in Europe that regulate how organizations collect, use, protect, and disclose personal data.

A European Union agency that manages EU trademarks and designs and supports intellectual-property enforcement work.
european-union
The European Union is a political and economic union of European countries that also creates cybersecurity and privacy rules.

Europol is the European Union’s law enforcement agency that helps member countries fight serious and organized crime.
evade detection technique
To evade detection means to hide malicious activity so security tools or analysts do not notice it.
evasion technique
A technique used by attackers to avoid detection by security tools like antivirus or firewalls.
evidence collection technique
Evidence collection is the process of gathering logs, files, screenshots, and other proof for an investigation or audit.
Examination Proctoring concept
Monitoring students during exams to help enforce test rules and prevent cheating.
executable image concept
A program file arranged in a format that an operating system can load and run.

An exploit path is the chain of steps an attacker could take to reach and abuse a vulnerability.

Exploit paths are the sequence of weaknesses or steps an attacker could use to break into or compromise a system.

Exploitability describes how easily an attacker can take advantage of a security weakness.
exploitation technique
Exploitation is taking advantage of a weakness in software or people to gain unauthorized access or control.

Exploited means attackers successfully took advantage of a weakness in software or a system.

Exploited in the wild means attackers are actively using a vulnerability against real targets, not just in a lab.

Export means sending goods, software, technology, or services from one country to another.

exposed credentials concept

Information that may have been viewed, copied, or made accessible to people who were not supposed to have it.
exposed open directory concept
An exposed open directory is a web-accessible folder that lists files publicly, often because a server was misconfigured.

exposed secrets concept

ExpressVPN is a commercial VPN service provider.

External Cybersecurity Specialists organization
Outside security experts hired to investigate, test, or help respond to a cyber incident.
External Provider concept
A separate company or service that performs work for an organization.
external service provider concept
A separate company or organization hired to provide technology or other services for an organization.
extortion concept

An extortion group is a criminal group that pressures victims to pay or cooperate by threatening harm such as leaking stolen data.
F1 organization
F1, or Formula 1, is an international top-level motor racing series.
f5

An NGINX configuration directive that sends requests to a backend application using FastCGI.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies are U.S. federal government agencies outside the military and intelligence community.

financial information concept

financial institutions organization

financial sector concept
The financial sector includes organizations and services involved in money, banking, investments, and payments.
financial services organization
Financial services are businesses such as banks, payment companies, insurers, and investment firms that manage money or financial transactions.

flaw concept

fraud concept

Official documents or details, such as passport or national-ID information, used to prove identity.

People who work for or hold positions in a government.

Governor’s Office of Information Technology organization
The Governor’s Office of Information Technology is a Colorado government organization that manages technology services for the state.

hackers concept

healthcare providers organization

i1 other

These are official records, such as passports or driver's licenses, used to prove who a person is.

identity documents concept

An identity provider is a service that verifies who a user is and lets them sign in to other apps or systems.

illegal API resellers concept
Illicit sellers who offer access to software interfaces or online services without authorization.

IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE concept

impersonate technique

impersonating technique
Pretending to be a trusted person, organization, or service in order to deceive someone.

impostors concept
Impostors are fake people, accounts, or projects pretending to be someone or something trusted.
in memory concept
In memory means something runs or exists in a computer’s temporary working memory rather than as a normal file on disk.
inbound concept

Inception Extortion Group threat-actor
A threat-actor group referenced in security reporting that uses extortion against victims.
Incident concept
A security incident is an event that may harm systems, data, or users and needs investigation or response.
Incident responders concept
Incident responders are specialists who investigate cyberattacks, contain damage, and help organizations recover safely.
incident response concept
Incident response is the process of investigating and handling a security problem after it is found.

An incident response plan is a prepared set of steps an organization follows when a cyberattack or major IT problem happens.
incidents concept
Incidents are security events that may harm systems, data, users, or business operations and need investigation or response.
indicators concept
Indicators are clues such as IP addresses, domains, file hashes, or behaviors that may point to malicious activity.
Indicators of Compromise concept
Indicators of Compromise are clues such as addresses, file names, or patterns that can show malicious activity happened.

Infected means a device or system has been compromised by malware or unauthorized code.

A computer or device that has been compromised by malicious software or an attacker.

information technology concept
Information technology is the use and management of computers, networks, software, and data in an organization.

infrastructure failures concept
Breakdowns in the underlying computers, networks, power, or services needed to keep a system running.
ingestion concept
Ingestion is the process of collecting data into a system so it can be stored, searched, or analyzed.

initial access method technique
An initial access method is the way an attacker first gets into a target system or network.
initial access vector technique

injection technique

intellectual property concept

Usernames, passwords, tokens, or other secrets used by an organization's internal accounts.

internal customer identification numbers concept

internal hosts and ports concept

internal services concept

internet-facing applications concept

internet-facing system concept

internet-facing systems concept

intrusion concept

intrusions concept

investigation concept
